stories.event: He stayed in the study hall on Yom Kippur eve instead of coming home as usual.
stories.turn: His waiting wife shed a tear of distress.
stories.outcome: The roof he sat on collapsed and he died.
stories.summary: Rav Rehumi used to come home every Yom Kippur eve, but one year he was absorbed in study and stayed away. His wife kept expecting him and, when he did not come, a tear fell from her eye. At that moment the roof under him collapsed and he died.

stories.event: He used to come home every Shabbat eve preceded by a pillar of fire, but one week he stayed at study.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, declared him dead and ordered his bed overturned.
stories.outcome: The ruler's mistaken words came true and Yehuda died.
stories.summary: Yehuda, Rabbi Yannai's son-in-law, came home every Friday at dusk with a pillar of fire before him. One day he stayed absorbed in study; Rabbi Yannai, missing the sign, said he must be dead and told them to overturn his bed. Like an error from a ruler, the statement took effect and Yehuda died.

stories.event: He arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Hiyya's family.
stories.turn: The bride died when the marriage contract was being written.
stories.outcome: Checking the genealogies, they found the families' differing Davidic descent.
stories.summary: Rabbi arranged a match for his son with Rabbi Hiyya's family, but the girl died as the ketubah was being written. Suspecting a flaw, they investigated the lineages and found Rabbi descended from David's wife Avital and Rabbi Hiyya from David's brother Shimi.

stories.event: Betrothed into Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family on condition of twelve years of study first, he saw the bride and cut it to six, then insisted on marrying first.
stories.turn: After twelve years away his wife became infertile.
stories.outcome: Rabbi weighed the bad options, the husband prayed, and she was cured.
stories.summary: Rabbi's son was to study twelve years before marrying, but on seeing the bride he reduced it to six and then chose to marry first, and his father reassured his embarrassment. He then studied twelve years and returned to find his wife infertile. Since divorce or a second wife would both shame her, he prayed for her and she was healed.

stories.event: He left for the study hall at the end of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding feast, refusing to wait for him.
stories.turn: He studied twelve years away.
stories.outcome: When he returned the city's paths had changed and he could not find his home.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai went off to study without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and stayed twelve years. When he came back the town had changed so much he did not know the way to his own house.

stories.event: Riding along the river, Rav Mesharshiyya and other rabbis on the far bank did not stand for him.
stories.turn: Abaye rebuked them, claiming he was their primary teacher.
stories.outcome: They said they had not noticed him.
stories.summary: Abaye rode a donkey along the Sagya River while Rav Mesharshiyya and other scholars sat on the opposite bank without rising. He asked whether he was not their primary teacher, owed standing at any distance. They answered that they had not even seen him.

stories.actor: Ravina and Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti
stories.event: A man passed Ravina without covering his head.
stories.turn: Ravina called him rude.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yirmeya suggested he was from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are so common people are less careful.
stories.summary: While Ravina sat before Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti, a man walked by bareheaded and Ravina remarked on his rudeness. Rabbi Yirmeya excused him: perhaps he came from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are so plentiful that people are lax about such honor.

stories.event: Rav Anan sent Rav Huna a familiar letter ('Huna our friend') asking him to give a woman a tenth of the estate.
stories.turn: Rav Huna, offended, sent back a sharp reply through Rav Sheshet under threat of excommunication.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva told Rav Anan he had overstepped by addressing Rav Huna as a peer.
stories.summary: Rav Anan wrote to Rav Huna as 'our friend' asking him to award a woman her dowry share. Rav Huna made Rav Sheshet deliver, on pain of excommunication, a curt reply asking 'Anan, Anan' whether from land or movables and who sits at the head in a house of marzeiha. Rav Sheshet apologetically delivered it; Rav Anan, puzzled, went to Mar Ukva, who told him that someone who does not know what marzeiha means has no business calling Rav Huna his friend.

stories.event: Funerals had become so costly that families abandoned their dead.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel instructed that he be buried in plain linen.
stories.outcome: Everyone followed his example, and simple burial became the norm.
stories.summary: Burial expenses had grown so burdensome that relatives would leave the dead and flee. Rabban Gamliel deliberately asked to be buried in simple linen garments. The whole people followed him, and in Rav Pappa's day even cheap rough cloth was used.

stories.actor: a millstone owner and his renter
stories.event: A man rented out a millstone in exchange for grinding services.
stories.turn: He became rich, bought his own mill and donkey, and demanded money instead.
stories.outcome: The renter refused, offering only to keep grinding as agreed.
stories.summary: A man let another use his millstone in return for grinding his grain. Later he grew wealthy, bought his own mill and donkey, and asked for cash rent. The renter answered that he had agreed to grind, not to pay.

stories.event: Wanting to give away many movables, he was told it could only be done by means of land.
stories.turn: He bought a beit sela of land and gave a portion with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels.
stories.outcome: He died and the Sages upheld his gift.
stories.summary: A Madonite in Jerusalem with much movable property wished to give it away and was told he had to transfer it along with land. He bought a rocky plot near Jerusalem, gave its northern part with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels to someone, and died. The Sages carried out his words.

stories.event: He wished to give away his many movables and was told it must be done through land.
stories.turn: He bought a beit rova and gave a square handbreadth with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels.
stories.outcome: He died and the Sages fulfilled his statement.
stories.summary: A man in Jerusalem, sick or healthy by different accounts, wanted to give away his movables and was told he needed land to do it. He acquired a small plot, assigned a handbreadth of it with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels to someone, and died. The Sages honored the gift.

stories.event: Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Yaakov bar Zavdi stood up for him as he passed while they studied.
stories.turn: He told them they need not have stood.
stories.outcome: He explained they were ordained and he was not, and Torah does not stand for its students.
stories.summary: Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Yaakov bar Zavdi were studying when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed and they rose for him. He objected that they were ordained Sages while he was only an associate, and that those engaged in Torah need not stand for its scholars.

stories.actor: the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
stories.event: The Sages awarded her four hundred gold coins a day for perfumes.
stories.turn: She responded with a sarcastic blessing.
stories.outcome: She told them to award the same to their daughters, and they answered Amen.
stories.summary: When the Sages set an allowance of four hundred gold coins for the widow's perfumes, Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter said, 'May you award this for your own daughters,' and they answered Amen.

stories.event: Leaving Jerusalem, he saw a young woman gathering barley from Arab animals' dung.
stories.turn: She revealed she was Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter, whose dowry he had signed as a million gold dinars.
stories.outcome: He wept and lamented Israel's fall when it does not do God's will.
stories.summary: Riding out of Jerusalem with his students, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai met a starving girl picking barley from dung, who covered herself with her hair and begged for support. She turned out to be the daughter of the wealthy Nakdimon ben Guryon, and reminded him he had signed her marriage contract. He recalled its million-dinar dowry, wept, and said that when Israel fails God it is handed over even to the animals of a lowly nation.

stories.actor: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok
stories.event: He saw Nakdimon's daughter gathering barley from between horses' hooves in Akko.
stories.turn: The sight moved him.
stories.outcome: He applied a verse from Song of Songs to her plight.
stories.summary: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok swore he had seen Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter picking barley from between horses' hooves in Akko. He recited a verse about her, reading it as following the flocks to feed her own body.

stories.actor: a dying father and his heirs
stories.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter.
stories.turn: The orphans divided the estate without giving her any palm tree.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled they must give her a tree and redivide the estate.
stories.summary: A man left a palm tree to his daughter, but his sons split the estate and gave her none. Rav Yosef compared it to the mishna's path case, but Abaye distinguished it and said the brothers must give her a tree and divide the property again.

stories.actor: a dying father's daughter and heirs
stories.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter but left only two half-trees.
stories.turn: Rav Ashi questioned whether two halves count as a palm tree.
stories.outcome: Rav Mordekhai reported Rava's view that they do.
stories.summary: A man promised his daughter a palm tree but died owning only halves of two trees, which the heirs offered her. Rav Ashi wondered whether that fulfilled the bequest, and Rav Mordekhai told him in Rava's name that people do call two halves a palm tree.

stories.event: She brought two maidservants into her marriage, and her husband took a second wife and gave her one of them.
stories.turn: The first wife cried out before Rava.
stories.outcome: Rava ignored her complaint.
stories.summary: A woman brought two maidservants as her dowry; her husband married another wife and assigned one maidservant to her. The first wife protested before Rava, who paid no attention, which observers took as a ruling on a husband's power over his wife's property.

stories.actor: a former captive and his mother
stories.event: A man casually remarked that he and his mother had been captives and he never left her.
stories.turn: His incidental remark came before Rabbi.
stories.outcome: Rabbi permitted his mother to marry a priest on that basis.
stories.summary: A man chatting offhandedly said he and his mother were taken captive and that whether drawing water or gathering wood his mind was always on her. On the strength of that unconsidered remark Rabbi allowed her to marry into the priesthood.

stories.event: He swore his wife's hand never left his during the gentiles' occupation of Jerusalem.
stories.turn: The Sages rejected his testimony since a man cannot testify for himself.
stories.outcome: He kept her in a separate house in his courtyard, never alone with her.
stories.summary: The priest Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav swore his wife had never left his side while gentiles held Jerusalem, but the Sages ruled one cannot testify about oneself, so she was forbidden to him. He did not divorce her; he gave her a house in his courtyard and arranged that she always came and went with her children so they were never secluded.

stories.actor: a widow at her husband's grave
stories.event: While mourning she had relations with a guard watching an executed man's body.
stories.turn: The body he was guarding was stolen.
stories.outcome: She removed her husband's body from his grave to replace it.
stories.summary: A woman mourning at her husband's grave became involved with a guard posted over a crucified body. When that body was taken, she disinterred her own husband so the guard could claim he had done his duty.

stories.event: Ten men carried out a woman on a bier as if she were dead.
stories.turn: They used the pretense to abuse her.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef cited it as proof a group is not deterred by shame.
stories.summary: There was an incident in which ten immoral men carried a woman out on a funeral bier and violated her together, showing that a group of such men does not restrain one another.

stories.event: A man testified that someone had presumptive priestly status.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ami asked whether reading first meant priest or great man, and learned a Levite read after him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated him to the priesthood.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Ami that someone was a priest because he read first in synagogue. Rabbi Ami asked whether that was due to priesthood or prominence, and was told a Levite read next. On that basis he recognized the man as a priest.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and a witness
stories.event: A man testified that someone was presumed a Levite because he read second.
stories.turn: Asked whether it was due to prominence, he said a priest had read before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi confirmed him as a Levite.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was a Levite because he read second in the synagogue. When asked if it was because of his stature, he answered that a priest read before him, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi accepted him as a Levite.

stories.event: Reish Lakish demanded proof of teruma distribution before accepting a priestly claim, and Rabbi Elazar challenged him.
stories.turn: Later Rabbi Yohanan gave the same reply in a similar case.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar for not citing Rabbi Yohanan's name.
stories.summary: When a man vouched for a priest because he read first, Reish Lakish asked whether he had seen him take teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar asked whether the priesthood ends where there is no threshing floor. Later, before Rabbi Yohanan, the same case arose and Rabbi Yohanan said the very same words. Reish Lakish looked angrily at Rabbi Elazar, rebuking him for quoting 'the smith's son' without attribution.

stories.event: Redeemed captive women were lodged in his attic and the ladder was removed.
stories.turn: Seized with desire for one, he lifted a huge ladder and began climbing, but halfway stopped himself and shouted 'Fire in Amram's house!'
stories.outcome: He made his evil inclination leave him as a pillar of fire and declared himself superior to it.
stories.summary: Captive women were housed in Rav Amram's upper floor with the ladder taken away. Overcome by one's beauty, he lifted a ladder ten men could not move and climbed, but halfway up braced himself and cried 'Fire!' The Sages came and said he shamed them; he replied better shame now than in the World-to-Come, then forced his evil inclination out as a pillar of fire, saying he, mere flesh, had beaten it.

stories.event: He mocked transgressors, and Satan appeared to him as a woman across a river.
stories.turn: He crossed by a rope bridge toward her.
stories.outcome: Halfway across Satan released him, saying only heaven's warning saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to scoff at sinners. Satan appeared as a woman on the far side of a river, and he started across a rope bridge after her. Halfway over Satan let him go, saying he would have ruined him if heaven had not proclaimed to be careful with Rabbi Meir.

stories.event: He mocked transgressors, and Satan appeared to him as a woman atop a palm tree.
stories.turn: He began climbing the tree.
stories.outcome: Halfway up Satan released him, citing heaven's protection of him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva likewise ridiculed sinners until Satan appeared as a woman at the top of a palm. He started climbing, and halfway up Satan let him go, saying only heaven's warning about Rabbi Akiva kept him from destroying him.

stories.event: He taunted Satan daily, and on Yom Kippur eve Satan came as a pauper and behaved repulsively at his table.
stories.turn: Satan feigned death and people accused Peleimu of murder, so he hid in the privy.
stories.outcome: Satan revealed himself and told him to say 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan' instead.
stories.summary: Peleimu used to say 'An arrow in Satan's eye.' On Yom Kippur eve Satan came as a poor man, demanded to eat inside and at the table, covered himself in sores and acted disgustingly, spat into a cup, and when rebuked collapsed as if dead. Hearing cries that Peleimu had killed a man, Peleimu hid in the bathroom; Satan followed, revealed himself, and told him to change his taunt to a prayer that God rebuke Satan.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi and his wife
stories.event: He prayed daily to be saved from the evil inclination.
stories.turn: His wife, overhearing, wondered why since he had withdrawn from her for years.
stories.outcome: Cut off at the window's edge.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi always prayed to be saved from the evil inclination. His wife heard and wondered why, since he had abstained from relations with her for years because of age. The story continues past the window.

stories.actor: a debtor's purchaser and a creditor
stories.event: A creditor repossessed one of two plots the debtor had sold for fifty each and came for the second.
stories.turn: The purchaser offered one hundred dinars to keep both.
stories.outcome: He told the creditor to take the plot at a hundred or take the money and leave.
stories.summary: A man owing one hundred dinars sold two small plots for fifty each. The creditor seized one and then came for the other. The buyer brought one hundred dinars and told him either accept the first plot as full payment or take the cash and give up both.

stories.event: A creditor seized the fifty-dinar plot left by a debtor who owed a hundred.
stories.turn: The orphans paid him fifty to redeem it.
stories.outcome: He seized it again for the rest of the debt.
stories.summary: A man died owing a hundred dinars and left land worth fifty. The creditor took it, the orphans paid fifty to get it back, and the creditor seized it again.

stories.event: Sent to betroth a woman to his son, he betrothed her to himself.
stories.turn: Her family would not give her to the son.
stories.outcome: He acted at once, fearing someone else would betroth her meanwhile.
stories.summary: Ravin the Pious went to arrange a betrothal for his son but married the woman himself. The Gemara explains her family refused the son, and he did not wait to inform him lest another man take her first.

stories.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
stories.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy land for him, and Rav bought it for himself.
stories.turn: The sellers were violent men who respected only Rav.
stories.outcome: Rav bought it immediately so no one else would.
stories.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a plot, but Rav bought it in his own name. The land lay among violent people who would deal with Rav but not with Rabba bar bar Hana, and Rav feared another buyer would take it if he delayed.

stories.event: Rabbi Abba bought land Rav Giddel was negotiating for.
stories.turn: Confronted by Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, Rabbi Abba said he had not known and offered it as a gift.
stories.outcome: Neither would take it, and it became known as the land of the Sages.
stories.summary: Rav Giddel was negotiating for a plot when Rabbi Abba bought it. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who took it to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha; at the Festival he asked Rabbi Abba about a poor man's loaf snatched by another, and Rabbi Abba called such a person wicked but said he had not known, and would give the land as a gift rather than sell his first purchase. Rav Giddel refused gifts and Rabbi Abba would not use it, so it was left as 'the Rabbis' land.'

stories.event: Pursued by many suitors, she claimed to be already betrothed.
stories.turn: Later she betrothed herself to someone.
stories.outcome: She explained to the Sages she had lied to fend off unworthy men, and she was believed.
stories.summary: An exceptionally beautiful woman, besieged by suitors, said she was already betrothed. Later she betrothed herself, and when the Sages asked why, she said her earlier claim was to repel unsuitable men and she accepted a worthy one. The Sages ruled that a woman who gives such a reason is believed.

stories.actor: Rav Huna and his son Rabba
stories.event: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son.
stories.turn: He did it to test whether Rabba would lose his temper.
stories.outcome: The test of filial honor was carried out (the Gemara then examines its permissibility).
stories.summary: Rav Huna ripped silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether he would grow angry, as a test of his respect for his father. The Gemara notes he had waived his honor in advance.

stories.actor: Rav Yehezkel and his son Rav Yehuda
stories.event: Rav Yehezkel taught his son Rami a ruling about mixed condemned prisoners.
stories.turn: His other son Rav Yehuda objected that the reasoning did not fit the wording.
stories.outcome: Rav Yehuda proposed teaching the case in reverse.
stories.summary: Rav Yehezkel taught Rami that if those sentenced to burning were mixed with those sentenced to stoning, all are stoned. His son Rav Yehuda said, 'Father, do not teach it so,' since the majority principle would suffice, and offered the reversed wording instead.

stories.event: After his death he returned home every Shabbat eve.
stories.turn: A maidservant told a knocking neighbor to be quiet because Rabbi was sitting there.
stories.outcome: Having been revealed, he never came again.
stories.summary: Rabbi asked that his lamp, table and bed be kept in place because he came home every Friday evening even after death. One Shabbat eve a neighbor knocked and the maid hushed her, saying Rabbi was sitting there. Once it was known, he stopped coming so as not to cast aspersions on earlier righteous men.

stories.event: Rabbi said these two attendants who served him in life would serve him in death.
stories.turn: People assumed he meant his burial, but the two died before him.
stories.outcome: They understood he meant serving him in the World-to-Come.
stories.summary: On his deathbed Rabbi said Yosef Heifani and Shimon Efrati, who served him in life, would serve him in death. People thought he meant they would bury him, but their biers went out before his, so they realized he meant the next world.

stories.event: A heavenly voice declared everyone at Rabbi's funeral destined for the World-to-Come, but a launderer who visited Rabbi daily had missed that day.
stories.turn: Hearing the news, he threw himself from a roof and died.
stories.outcome: A heavenly voice declared him too destined for the World-to-Come.
stories.summary: On the day of Rabbi's funeral a heavenly voice promised the World-to-Come to all present. A launderer who came to Rabbi every day had not come that day; on hearing, he climbed to a roof, fell and died. A heavenly voice proclaimed that he too had a place in the World-to-Come.

stories.event: The creditor seized the orphans' fifty-dinar plot, they paid fifty to redeem it, and he seized it again.
stories.turn: They complained to Abaye.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled the repossession lawful, since their payment was a mitzva toward the debt.
stories.summary: A man died owing a hundred dinars and left land worth fifty. The creditor took it, the orphans bought it back for fifty, and he took it again. Abaye told them paying a father's debt is a mitzva they had fulfilled, but the land was still liened, so the creditor acted lawfully.

stories.actor: a man who sold his mother's ketubah
stories.event: He sold rights to his mother's marriage contract, disclaiming liability if she objected.
stories.turn: His mother died without objecting, and he himself contested the sale.
stories.outcome: Rava rejected his claim, since he guaranteed against his own objection.
stories.summary: A man sold the future rights to his mother's ketubah, saying he would not repay if his mother objected. She died without objecting, but he then challenged the sale himself. Rami bar Hama thought he stood in her place, but Rava said he had surely guaranteed against his own reneging.
